name: Barrow-in-Furness
title: Barrow-in-Furness Ship Gauging | UTM at the Commercial Docks
description: Ultrasonic thickness measurement at Barrow-in-Furness for offshore wind vessels, coasters and project cargo ships: hull, tanks, decks and piping alongside.
h1: Thickness Measurement for Commercial Ships at the Port of Barrow
intro: Barrow-in-Furness, on the Furness peninsula in Cumbria, is best known for the BAE Systems shipyard that builds the Royal Navy's submarines. Beside it, Associated British Ports runs a commercial port serving offshore wind farms in the Irish Sea, the energy industry around Morecambe Bay, and bulk and project cargoes. Ships here lie in enclosed docks entered through a lock from the Walney Channel. Our technicians come from India for each job and work only on commercial vessels in the port, never on the naval programme.

highlights.h: Offshore wind's base on the coast
highlights.p: Operations and maintenance bases for the wind farms off Walney Island work from Barrow, so crew transfer and offshore support vessels are regular visitors. Between rotations, their hulls, tanks, deck cranes and boarding-equipment foundations can be gauged and checked for cracks alongside.

Ships pass from the Walney Channel through a lock into Ramsden Dock and the inner basins, where the water stays at one level. A moored vessel lies steady whatever the large tide outside is doing, so a tank programme can run across several days without disturbance.

highlights.h: Kept apart from the submarine yard
highlights.p: The BAE Systems site shares the dock estate but is a restricted naval facility. Our work at Barrow is limited to commercial ships at ABP's quays, arranged through their owners and agents and under the port's own access controls.

port.h: Barrow: a dock port between Walney Island and the Furness peninsula
p: Barrow-in-Furness grew in the nineteenth century from a small village into an industrial town built on iron, steel, shipbuilding and its docks. The port lies behind Walney Island, a long, low island that shelters the Walney Channel from the Irish Sea, and ships approach from Morecambe Bay along a buoyed channel before locking into the docks. There are four main basins, Ramsden, Buccleuch, Cavendish and Devonshire Docks, and part of the estate is used by BAE Systems, whose Devonshire Dock Hall is one of the largest shipbuilding halls in Europe. The tidal range in the approaches is large and the channel is prone to silting, so arrivals and departures are planned around high water with a pilot on board and tugs on hand.

The commercial port, run by Associated British Ports, has found new work in energy. Offshore wind farms west of Walney and in the eastern Irish Sea are serviced from bases in the docks, with crew transfer vessels and offshore support ships coming and going regularly. The port also handles cargo for the gas industry around Morecambe Bay, bulk and general cargoes, and project loads, including heavy equipment for the shipyard and for energy sites. Specialist ships that carry nuclear materials for the Sellafield site have been based at Barrow for many years. In 2025 the port was granted the title Royal Port of Barrow in recognition of its part in national security, and ABP has published a long-term plan to grow its energy, defence and cargo business.

The ships calling at Barrow are a specialised mix. Crew transfer vessels are small and fast and take technicians out to the wind farms day after day; offshore support and service vessels stay at sea for longer rotations; cargo ships and coasters call for bulk and project loads; and the shipyard brings in heavy-lift vessels with equipment. For gauging, the important point is that many of these vessels return to Barrow often and spend time in the enclosed docks between trips, which gives access without the pressure of a quick cargo turnaround. Winter weather in the Irish Sea also increases downtime for the smallest vessels, and the days when crew transfer vessels cannot sail are often given over to maintenance and inspection.

facilities.h: Where ships are gauged at Barrow
p: Commercial work takes place at ABP's quays in Ramsden Dock and the adjoining basins. Offshore support and crew transfer vessels lie at their operators' berths between trips, where hull plating, fuel and water tanks, deck structure, boarding-equipment foundations and piping can be gauged and checked for cracks. Cargo ships and coasters at the general cargo berths are worked around loading and discharge, with holds measured as they empty. The water in the docks stays at a constant level, so access is steady once a vessel is moored and the crew has prepared the spaces.

Barrow's commercial docks are not a merchant ship-repair centre, so vessels from the port are docked at yards on the Mersey, in Northern Ireland, in Scotland or further afield. The BAE Systems shipyard and its facilities are reserved for the naval programme and play no part in any commercial job. For owners, the realistic Barrow work is in-service gauging alongside, used to plan the next docking or to document condition for a charter, a sale or a survey. A vessel laid up between offshore contracts gives the longest window and allows every tank to be opened in turn.
list: Offshore wind operator berths — hull, tank, deck and boarding-equipment foundation gauging on crew transfer and support vessels between trips.
Ramsden Dock cargo quays — hold, hatch coaming and ballast tank readings on coasters and cargo ships during loading or discharge.
Project cargo berths — deck and crane pedestal checks on heavy-lift ships while equipment is landed.
Lay-by berths in the inner basins — longer condition surveys on vessels waiting between contracts.
Weather downtime alongside — tank and piping programmes on small vessels kept in port by Irish Sea conditions.

context.h: Security, regulation and the energy trade at Barrow
p: Barrow is unusual among commercial ports because of the defence and nuclear activity around it. The submarine programme and the movement of nuclear materials bring extra security controls on parts of the dock estate on top of the normal ISPS regime, and visitors are expected to follow site rules to the letter. For commercial ships, port state control is carried out by the Maritime and Coastguard Agency under Paris MoU procedures applied through UK law, and visiting ships are expected to carry an Inventory of Hazardous Materials under the ship recycling rules the UK retained from EU legislation.

Offshore wind vessels follow their own rules. Crew transfer vessels are usually small and certified under workboat or high-speed craft codes administered by the flag state, while larger service and support vessels follow class rules and the full survey cycle. Either way, operators are under pressure to keep vessels available through the year, so inspection is planned for weather downtime or scheduled maintenance. Thickness readings on hulls, tanks and boarding-equipment foundations, and crack checks on welded structure that takes repeated impact from turbine landings, help them avoid unplanned time off hire.

jobs.p: Most Barrow jobs come from offshore energy operators and from owners of cargo ships calling with bulk or project loads. Offshore work is planned around vessel rotations and weather: a crew transfer vessel kept in port by a gale is a chance to gauge her hull and tanks, while an offshore support vessel between contracts can have a full survey. Cargo ship work is planned around loading and discharge in the docks. Every job is for a commercial vessel and is arranged through the owner or agent, with access under the port's security rules and passes confirmed before the team leaves India.
list: Hull and tank gauging on a crew transfer vessel during weather downtime between wind farm trips.
MPI on the bow fender structure of a crew transfer vessel after repeated turbine landings.
Condition survey of an offshore support vessel between contracts: tanks, deck, crane foundations and piping.
Hold and ballast tank readings on a coaster or cargo ship while she loads in Ramsden Dock.
Deck and crane pedestal checks on a heavy-lift ship landing project cargo.

logistics: Manchester Airport is the usual international gateway; from there the team takes the train north through Lancaster and around the Furness coast to Barrow, or travels by road. Technicians come from India on UK visas, and because Barrow's security arrangements add a step, we allow extra time between confirming a job and boarding. The vessel's owner or agent arranges port passes with ABP and confirms the berth, the lock time and any additional site rules before the team travels.

faqs.q: Do you work on submarines or at the BAE Systems shipyard?
faqs.a: No. The shipyard and the submarine programme are a restricted naval site and are not part of our work. At Barrow we gauge commercial vessels at Associated British Ports' quays, such as offshore wind vessels, cargo ships and coasters, under the port's normal access arrangements and with passes arranged by the vessel's owner or agent.

faqs.q: Can crew transfer vessels be gauged at Barrow without losing working days?
faqs.a: Usually, by using weather downtime and planned maintenance periods. When conditions keep a crew transfer vessel in port, the team can gauge hull plating, tanks and foundations alongside and check bow fenders and welded structure for cracks with magnetic particle inspection. We agree a standing scope with the operator and fit it to the days the team is on site.

faqs.q: How do ships get into the docks at Barrow?
faqs.a: Through a lock from the Walney Channel, timed around high water. The approach crosses a large tidal range and a channel that needs regular maintenance, so arrivals and departures follow the tide and the pilot's advice. Once inside, the water level stays constant, and gauging continues through the tide without disturbing moorings or access to the ship.

faqs.q: Where are vessels from Barrow drydocked?
faqs.a: At yards elsewhere, on the Mersey, in Northern Ireland, in Scotland or further afield, depending on size and availability. We gauge at Barrow beforehand, so the owner can give the yard a list of plating and piping to renew, and the docking period can be planned around known work rather than findings made once the vessel is dry.
